subject: biology

items.q: On pre-biotic Earth, ultraviolet light penetrated to the surface far more than it does today. What is the reason for this?
items.correct: There was no free oxygen, so no ozone could form to absorb the radiation.
items.misconception: The methane and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere had destroyed the ozone layer.
items.why: Ozone is met in geography and chemistry as 'the ozone layer', something damaged by CFCs and pollutants, so students picture it as an independent shield and do not connect its existence to the presence of oxygen. Ozone is made from oxygen. Ultraviolet light splits O₂ molecules and the oxygen atoms combine with O₂ to form O₃, which then absorbs ultraviolet radiation. Pre-biotic Earth lacked free oxygen and therefore lacked ozone, so ultraviolet light penetrated to the surface.
items.specStatementText: Early Earth's conditions let carbon compounds form without life
items.random_wrong: Free oxygen was used up oxidizing methane before it could form ozone.

items.q: A variety of carbon compounds is thought to have formed spontaneously on pre-biotic Earth. Why do the same processes not produce these compounds naturally on Earth today?
items.correct: The atmosphere now contains free oxygen, which oxidizes such compounds as they form.
items.misconception: Carbon compounds can only be produced by the metabolism of living cells.
items.why: The word 'organic' means 'from living things' in everyday use and organic compounds are often introduced at GCSE as the compounds found in living organisms, so students absorb the old idea of vitalism – that organic matter needs a living source. Carbon compounds form by ordinary chemistry whenever the reactants and an energy source are present. On pre-biotic Earth, ultraviolet light, lightning and heat acting on gases such as methane and ammonia are thought to have produced amino acids and other carbon compounds, as the Miller–Urey experiment later demonstrated in the laboratory.
items.specStatementText: Early Earth's conditions let carbon compounds form without life
items.random_wrong: Oxygen was present then as now, so something else must have stopped the processes.

items.q: Which statement gives a reason that viruses are considered to be non-living?
items.correct: They carry out no metabolism and can only replicate using a host cell.
items.misconception: They are cells that are too small to hold the organelles needed for metabolism.
items.why: At GCSE, viruses and bacteria are compared mainly by size and by whether antibiotics work, so students order them as 'big cell, small cell, very small cell' rather than recognising that a virus has no cellular structure at all. A virus consists of DNA or RNA enclosed in a protein capsid, sometimes with a lipid envelope taken from its host. It has no cytoplasm, no ribosomes and no metabolic enzymes, so it cannot carry out the functions of life. This is one of the reasons viruses are considered non-living.
items.specStatementText: The cell is the smallest thing that keeps itself alive
items.random_wrong: They are not whole organisms, and only complete organisms are living.

items.q: Which of these is the smallest unit that can sustain itself as living, given only nutrients and a source of energy?
items.correct: A free-living bacterium
items.misconception: A whole multicellular animal
items.why: 'Living things' at primary and lower-secondary level always means organisms – plants and animals – and cells are introduced as 'building blocks', a phrase that suggests inert bricks. A cell carries out metabolism, grows, responds, maintains its internal conditions and reproduces by division, so it satisfies the criteria for life. Unicellular organisms such as bacteria are single cells that live independently, showing that the cell, not the multicellular organism, is the smallest self-sustaining unit of life.
items.specStatementText: The cell is the smallest thing that keeps itself alive
items.random_wrong: A virus inside a host cell

items.q: Which set of processes is regarded as the necessary requirements for the evolution of the first cells?
items.correct: Catalysis, self-replication of molecules, self-assembly and the emergence of compartmentalization
items.misconception: A single improbable chance event assembling a complete cell with all of its parts at once
items.why: In everyday language 'spontaneous' suggests something sudden and complete, and the popular argument that a cell could no more assemble by chance than a whirlwind could build an aircraft presents the origin of cells as a single lucky accident. Scientists do not propose that a complete cell assembled by chance. The requirements for the first cells – catalysis, self-replication of molecules, self-assembly and the emergence of compartmentalization – are each processes that can happen spontaneously, and the first cells are thought to have emerged gradually as these processes combined, with natural selection favouring the more successful protocells.
items.specStatementText: Why the first cells are hard to explain
items.random_wrong: Formation of DNA, then transcription and translation, before any membrane had formed

items.q: A student claims that the hypothesis that the first cells arose spontaneously on pre-biotic Earth is not scientific, because the event cannot be observed. Which response is the best evaluation of this claim?
items.correct: It is testable indirectly, though hard to test because the exact conditions cannot be replicated.
items.misconception: The claim is correct, because an event that cannot be directly observed or repeated lies outside science.
items.why: School science presents 'the scientific method' as observing and repeating experiments, so an event four billion years ago that cannot be repeated seems to fall outside science altogether. Scientific claims must be testable, but testing can be indirect. Origin-of-cells hypotheses predict, for example, that carbon compounds form under simulated early-Earth conditions, that fatty acids self-assemble into vesicles, and that RNA can catalyse reactions – all of which have been tested. Scientists struggle with these hypotheses because the exact conditions on pre-biotic Earth cannot be replicated and the first protocells did not fossilize, but difficulty of testing is not the same as untestability.
items.specStatementText: Why the first cells are hard to explain
items.random_wrong: The claim is wrong, because the Miller–Urey experiment has already confirmed how the first cells formed.

items.q: In the Miller–Urey experiment, a mixture of methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour was exposed to electrical sparks for a week. Which conclusion is supported by the products that were found?
items.correct: Amino acids and other carbon compounds can form abiotically under such conditions.
items.misconception: Living cells can form from inorganic molecules given an energy source and enough time.
items.why: Popular summaries describe the experiment as 'creating life in a test tube', and students conflate the origin of carbon compounds with the origin of cells because both are covered under 'origin of life'. The experiment showed that carbon compounds needed by life, including amino acids, can form spontaneously from inorganic molecules under conditions that may have existed on pre-biotic Earth. It provides evidence for the pre-biotic origin of carbon compounds only; the later steps – polymerization, self-replication, self-assembly and compartmentalization – were not demonstrated.
items.specStatementText: Miller and Urey showed carbon compounds can form abiotically
items.random_wrong: The twenty amino acids used in proteins are the only products that such conditions make.

items.q: Geologists now think that the early atmosphere contained more carbon dioxide and nitrogen, and less methane and ammonia, than the mixture Miller and Urey used. What is the best evaluation of the experiment in the light of this?
items.correct: The mixture was a limitation, but the finding that such compounds can form abiotically still stands.
items.misconception: The experiment has been disproved, so it provides no evidence about the origin of carbon compounds on early Earth.
items.why: Students learn that a flawed method invalidates a conclusion, and they treat an evaluation as a verdict of 'right or wrong' rather than a weighing of what the evidence does and does not support. Evaluation means weighing strengths against limitations. The revised view of the early atmosphere – more carbon dioxide and nitrogen, less methane and ammonia – limits how closely the original experiment modelled early Earth, but the experiment still established that amino acids form from inorganic gases given an energy source, and experiments using other plausible mixtures have produced amino acids too.
items.specStatementText: Miller and Urey showed carbon compounds can form abiotically
items.random_wrong: The composition of the mixture does not matter, because the experiment proved how life began in any case.

items.q: Fatty acids added to water at a suitable pH coalesce into spherical bilayers, forming vesicles. What causes this to happen spontaneously?
items.correct: The molecules are amphipathic: hydrophobic tails are excluded from the water while hydrophilic heads stay in contact with it.
items.misconception: The molecules are entirely hydrophobic, so they separate from the water and pack into a solid droplet of lipid.
items.why: Students have seen oil separating from water and learn that lipids are hydrophobic, so they picture fatty acids as wholly water-repelling and do not consider the polar carboxyl group. A fatty acid is amphipathic: its carboxyl head is hydrophilic and its hydrocarbon tail is hydrophobic. In water the molecules arrange themselves so that the heads contact water and the tails are hidden from it, giving a bilayer that closes into a hollow sphere – a vesicle with water inside as well as outside, not a solid droplet.
items.specStatementText: Fatty acids self-assemble into vesicles
items.random_wrong: Strong bonds form between neighbouring hydrocarbon tails, pulling the molecules together into a closed layer.

items.q: Why was the formation of membrane-bound compartments a necessary step in the origin of cells?
items.correct: It allowed the chemistry inside the compartment to become different from that of the outside.
items.misconception: It shielded the enclosed molecules from the ultraviolet light that reached the surface.
items.why: At GCSE the cell membrane is described as something that 'protects the cell' and 'holds it together', so students carry that protective image over and do not think about concentration and chemical difference. The IB guide states that a membrane-bound compartment is needed to allow internal chemistry to become different from that outside. A thin bilayer is not a shield against ultraviolet light; its importance is that it keeps self-replicating molecules and their products together at higher concentrations, so that a distinct internal chemistry can develop and be selected for.
items.specStatementText: Fatty acids self-assemble into vesicles
items.random_wrong: It provided a solid droplet of lipid inside which the first chemical reactions could occur.

items.q: Why is RNA, rather than DNA, presumed to have been the first genetic material?
items.correct: RNA can be replicated and is catalytic, so it could serve as both genes and enzymes.
items.misconception: RNA formed as single-stranded copies made from the very first DNA molecules to exist.
items.why: The flow of information from DNA to RNA to protein is taught with DNA as the master copy and RNA as its messenger, so students assume this order reflects the order in which the molecules evolved. DNA can only be replicated and expressed with the help of enzymes, so a DNA-first origin faces the problem of which came first, the genes or the enzymes they encode. RNA avoids the problem because it can both carry information and catalyse reactions, which is why RNA is presumed to have been the first genetic material, with DNA taking over the role of information storage later.
items.specStatementText: RNA was probably the first genetic material
items.random_wrong: RNA is simpler than DNA, so it is more stable and survived for longer in the early oceans.

items.q: In ribosomes, the formation of peptide bonds between amino acids is catalysed by ribosomal RNA. Why is this significant for hypotheses about the origin of cells?
items.correct: It shows that RNA can catalyse reactions, as presumed for the earliest cells.
items.misconception: It shows that RNA is more stable than DNA, which is why it survived from the earliest cells.
items.why: Students assume that the earliest molecule must have been the most durable one and equate 'single-stranded and simpler' with 'more stable'. RNA is in fact less stable than DNA: the extra hydroxyl group on ribose makes it more easily broken down, which is one reason DNA later took over long-term information storage. The argument for RNA rests not on stability but on its ability to be both replicated and catalytic, and on the survival of ribozymes such as the ribosome's peptidyl transferase.
items.specStatementText: RNA was probably the first genetic material
items.random_wrong: It shows that rRNA must be a protein, since only proteins can act as catalysts.

items.q: Which evidence supports the existence of a last universal common ancestor (LUCA)?
items.correct: The same genetic code and some shared genes are found in all organisms.
items.misconception: All organisms carry identical DNA sequences in each of their genes.
items.why: In the media 'genetic code' is used loosely to mean an organism's DNA sequence, so 'the code is universal' is heard as 'the DNA is the same everywhere'. The genetic code is the dictionary that translates codons into amino acids, and it is shared by all life. Genes are the sentences written with that dictionary and differ between organisms. Some genes are shared across all organisms, and this is a separate piece of evidence for LUCA alongside the universal code.
items.specStatementText: All living things share one last common ancestor
items.random_wrong: Fossils of LUCA itself have been identified in the oldest rocks on Earth.

items.q: Codon UGG specifies tryptophan in bacteria, fungi, plants and animals alike. Why is this kind of observation taken as evidence for a common ancestor of all life?
items.correct: Codon assignments are largely arbitrary, so a shared code is best explained by a single ancestor.
items.misconception: The code is the only one that is chemically possible, so every organism that evolved had to use it.
items.why: Students expect chemistry to fix biological outcomes, and complementary base pairing, which is chemically determined, is easily confused with the codon-to-amino-acid assignments, which are not. Which codon specifies which amino acid is set by the tRNA molecules and the enzymes that load them, not by any chemical necessity. This is shown by the minor variations in the code in mitochondria and some organisms, and by laboratory cells engineered to use altered codes. A largely arbitrary convention shared by all life points to a single origin.
items.specStatementText: All living things share one last common ancestor
items.random_wrong: It shows that all organisms have the same genes, inherited without change from LUCA.

items.q: It is considered likely that other forms of life evolved on early Earth in addition to the lineage leading to LUCA. Why do none of them have living descendants today?
items.correct: They became extinct through competition from LUCA and its descendants.
items.misconception: They were wiped out by an asteroid impact before LUCA had appeared on Earth.
items.why: Extinction is introduced through the dinosaurs and mass extinction events, so students associate it with disasters rather than with the everyday process of being outcompeted. Most extinctions result from competition and changing conditions rather than from catastrophes. The IB guide includes the likelihood that other forms of life evolved on early Earth but became extinct because LUCA and its descendants outcompeted them, which is why only one lineage has living descendants.
items.specStatementText: All living things share one last common ancestor
items.random_wrong: It cannot be known, because unobserved events on early Earth lie outside science.

items.q: Stromatolites and microfossils in rocks from Western Australia are among the oldest evidence of cells. Which approach is used to estimate their age?
items.correct: Radiometric dating of the rock using isotopes with very long half-lives
items.misconception: Carbon-14 dating of the carbon left in the fossilized cells themselves
items.why: Carbon-14 dating is the only radiometric method met at GCSE and it is applied to archaeological remains, so it becomes 'the' scientific dating method in students' minds. Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5 700 years, so after 50 000 years too little remains to measure. Rocks billions of years old are dated using isotopes with half-lives of hundreds of millions to billions of years, such as uranium-238 decaying to lead-206. Fossils are dated from the age of the rock layers around them.
items.specStatementText: How the dates of first cells and LUCA are estimated
items.random_wrong: Sequencing the DNA preserved in the fossils and applying a molecular clock

items.q: Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago. The oldest widely accepted fossil cells are about 3.5 billion years old, and molecular clock estimates place LUCA at roughly 4 billion years ago. Which interpretation is valid?
items.correct: The dates are compatible: fossils give a minimum age for life, while molecular clock dates carry wide uncertainty.
items.misconception: The molecular clock date must be wrong, because the fossil gives the exact date at which life began on Earth.
items.why: The word 'clock' suggests precision, and dates in textbooks are printed as single numbers without error ranges. A molecular clock converts the number of sequence differences between lineages into time using an assumed rate of change, calibrated against fossils. Rates vary between genes and lineages, so estimates for events as ancient as LUCA carry uncertainties of hundreds of millions of years. Fossil dates give a minimum age for life and the two approaches are used together rather than one being exact.
items.specStatementText: How the dates of first cells and LUCA are estimated
items.random_wrong: The fossil date is unreliable, because carbon-14 dating cannot be used to measure ages of 3.5 billion years.

items.q: Which pair of findings provides evidence that LUCA evolved in the vicinity of hydrothermal vents?
items.correct: Microfossils in ancient seafloor vent precipitates, and conserved genes across all life that fit vent conditions
items.misconception: Photosynthetic microfossils in rocks formed in shallow sunlit water, and light-harvesting genes shared by all organisms
items.why: Darwin's 'warm little pond' is the image most students have met, and GCSE ecology presents photosynthesis as the foundation of every ecosystem, so sunlight seems indispensable to life. Fossilized evidence from ancient seafloor vent precipitates and genomic analysis of conserved genes both point to LUCA living near hydrothermal vents, obtaining energy from reactions involving hydrogen and carbon dioxide in the absence of light and oxygen. Photosynthesis evolved later in one lineage of LUCA's descendants.
items.specStatementText: Evidence that LUCA lived near hydrothermal vents
items.random_wrong: DNA sequenced from vent microfossils, and its close match to the genomes of bacteria living at vents today

items.q: Genomic analysis identified genes that are conserved across both bacteria and archaea. Their protein products enable life without oxygen, at high temperature, and using hydrogen and carbon dioxide as sources of energy and carbon. What does this suggest about LUCA?
items.correct: LUCA lived in a hot, anaerobic environment such as a hydrothermal vent on the seafloor.
items.misconception: LUCA lived in an atmosphere already rich in oxygen, since these genes are still in use today.
items.why: In everyday language 'air' means something you can breathe, and students meet oxygen as a permanent 21% of the atmosphere without ever being told that it is a product of life. Photosynthesis is learned as a process, not as an event in Earth's history. Pre-biotic Earth had no free oxygen. Oxygen is chemically reactive and did not persist in the atmosphere until photosynthetic organisms produced it faster than it was removed, long after the first cells appeared. The absence of oxygen also meant the absence of ozone, so ultraviolet light reached the surface, and it meant that carbon compounds formed spontaneously were not oxidized.
items.specStatementText: Evidence that LUCA lived near hydrothermal vents
items.random_wrong: LUCA lived in sunlit surface water and obtained its energy by photosynthesis.

items.q: Why were temperatures on early Earth higher than today?
items.correct: Because the atmosphere contained higher concentrations of carbon dioxide and methane, which are greenhouse gases that trap heat.
items.misconception: Early Earth was hot simply because the planet had not yet cooled from its formation, and heat explains all the other unusual conditions too.
items.why: Students picture the young Earth as a molten ball from images of its formation, so residual heat seems an obvious cause and they reach for it to explain temperature, ultraviolet light and chemical reactivity alike. The IB guide attributes the higher temperatures to the higher concentrations of carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere, which absorb infrared radiation and warm the surface. Ultraviolet penetration is a separate consequence of the lack of ozone, not of temperature.
items.specStatementText: Early Earth's conditions let carbon compounds form without life
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are viruses living organisms?
items.correct: No. Viruses are considered non-living because they have no metabolism of their own, are not made of cells, and can only replicate by using the machinery of a host cell.
items.misconception: Viruses are alive because they have genes, reproduce and evolve, and 'kill' or 'die' like other organisms.
items.why: News reports describe viruses as things that 'spread', 'attack' and 'are killed', and at GCSE viruses are grouped with bacteria, fungi and protists as pathogens or microorganisms, so students treat them as one more kind of living microbe. Reproduction and evolution are not enough on their own. A virus outside a host is an inert particle of nucleic acid and protein: it carries out no metabolism, cannot grow, respond or maintain itself, and it does not reproduce itself – the host cell's enzymes and ribosomes make new virus particles. Cells are the smallest units that are self-sustaining, and viruses fall below that threshold.
items.specStatementText: The cell is the smallest thing that keeps itself alive
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a mitochondrion, a ribosome or a DNA molecule alive?
items.correct: No. Organelles and molecules carry out parts of the functions of life but none can sustain itself outside a cell; the cell is the smallest unit of self-sustaining life.
items.misconception: Parts of cells are themselves alive – mitochondria are living because they respire and have their own DNA, and DNA is 'the molecule of life'.
items.why: Mitochondria are described as 'powerhouses' with their own DNA that once were free-living bacteria, and DNA is called the molecule of life, so students transfer the property of being alive down to the components of the cell. Being alive means being able to sustain all the functions of life – metabolism, growth, response, homeostasis and reproduction – independently. A mitochondrion depends on the cell for most of its proteins and cannot survive or reproduce outside it; a DNA molecule does nothing by itself. Only at the level of the whole cell are all the functions of life present together.
items.specStatementText: The cell is the smallest thing that keeps itself alive
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can cells still form spontaneously from non-living matter today?
items.correct: No. Cells are currently produced only by division of pre-existing cells.
items.misconception: If cells arose spontaneously once, they must still be forming from non-living material now, for example in ponds or in decaying food.
items.why: The everyday experience of mould and microbes 'appearing' in food and water suggests that life springs from non-living matter, and students reason that a process that happened on early Earth must be a general natural process still going on. Every cell observed today has come from the division of a pre-existing cell. The spontaneous origin of cells is thought to have required conditions that no longer exist, such as an atmosphere without free oxygen and an environment free of living organisms that would consume newly formed carbon compounds. This is why explaining the origin of the first cells is a challenge and why the hypothesis is hard to test.
items.specStatementText: Why the first cells are hard to explain
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which carbon compounds formed in the Miller–Urey experiment?
items.correct: A mixture of many carbon compounds, including several of the amino acids used in proteins, but also amino acids and other compounds that are not found in living organisms.
items.misconception: The experiment produced exactly the twenty amino acids used to build proteins, and nothing else.
items.why: Students meet 'amino acids' only as the twenty building blocks of proteins, so 'amino acids were formed' is heard as 'the twenty amino acids were formed'. Amino acid is a chemical class, not a list of twenty. Miller identified a handful of protein amino acids such as glycine and alanine, together with amino acids not used in proteins and a range of other carbon compounds; later reanalysis found more than twenty amino acids in his samples. That the products were an undirected mixture is one of the limitations to weigh when evaluating the experiment.
items.specStatementText: Miller and Urey showed carbon compounds can form abiotically
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do enzymes or living cells have to be present for a membrane to form?
items.correct: No. Fatty acids coalesce into bilayer vesicles spontaneously in water, driven by the exclusion of hydrophobic tails from water; no enzymes or cells are needed.
items.misconception: Membranes can only be made by living cells, so a membrane could not have existed until after the first cell.
items.why: Students learn that cell membranes are made in the endoplasmic reticulum and that cells need enzymes to build their structures, so a membrane appearing without a cell seems impossible. Self-assembly is one of the requirements for the origin of cells precisely because it needs no enzymes. Amphipathic molecules in water spontaneously form bilayers and vesicles, so membrane-bound compartments could arise before cells and provide the enclosure within which cellular chemistry evolved.
items.specStatementText: Fatty acids self-assemble into vesicles
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are all biological catalysts proteins?
items.correct: No. Some RNA molecules, called ribozymes, are catalysts; the ribosomal RNA that forms peptide bonds during translation is one example.
items.misconception: All enzymes are proteins, so the ribosome's catalytic work must be done by its proteins and RNA is only a structural scaffold.
items.why: 'Enzymes are proteins' is a GCSE definition that is repeated until it seems a law, and ribosomal proteins are named in diagrams while the RNA is drawn as an unlabelled framework. Most enzymes are proteins, but catalytic activity is a property of shape and chemistry, not of proteins alone. In the ribosome the peptidyl transferase reaction that joins amino acids is catalysed by ribosomal RNA in the large subunit, which makes the ribosome a ribozyme and a surviving relic of an RNA world.
items.specStatementText: RNA was probably the first genetic material
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Was LUCA the first living cell?
items.correct: No. LUCA is the most recent ancestor shared by all organisms alive today; other forms of life probably evolved before or alongside it but became extinct.
items.misconception: LUCA was the very first cell, the original organism from which everything started.
items.why: 'The ancestor of all life' sounds like 'the beginning of life', and family-tree diagrams place LUCA at the root, so students read the root as the starting point rather than as the last shared node. LUCA is defined by being the last common ancestor, not the first organism. The IB guide includes the likelihood that other forms of life evolved but became extinct through competition from LUCA and its descendants. Evidence for LUCA – the universal genetic code and shared genes – comes from comparing living organisms; no fossil of LUCA has been identified.
items.specStatementText: All living things share one last common ancestor
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: For how much of Earth's history has life existed?
items.correct: For most of it: Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago and cells existed by about 3.5 billion years ago, so life has been evolving for well over three billion years.
items.misconception: Life is a comparatively recent arrival on Earth, appearing a few hundred million years ago when the familiar fossils begin.
items.why: The fossils students know – trilobites, dinosaurs, early humans – all date from the last 540 million years, so the fossil record seems to begin there and the billions of years of microbial life leave no impression. Life has existed for around 80% of Earth's history. The first cells appeared within the first billion years, and for most of the time since then life consisted only of microorganisms. Appreciating this immense span of time is essential for understanding how much evolutionary change has been possible.
items.specStatementText: How the dates of first cells and LUCA are estimated
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where does the genomic evidence about LUCA come from?
items.correct: From comparing the genomes of living organisms to find genes conserved across bacteria and archaea, which are inferred to have been present in LUCA.
items.misconception: Scientists extracted and sequenced DNA from the ancient microfossils, so we know LUCA's genome directly.
items.why: Films and news stories about ancient DNA from mammoths and Neanderthals give the impression that DNA can be recovered from any fossil, however old. DNA breaks down within a few million years at most, so nothing survives from fossils billions of years old, and no fossil has been identified as LUCA. Genomic analysis instead compares the genomes of living species: sequences conserved across all of them were probably present in their common ancestor, and the functions of those genes reveal the kind of environment LUCA lived in.
items.specStatementText: Evidence that LUCA lived near hydrothermal vents
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What holds the hydrophobic tails of fatty acids together in a bilayer?
items.correct: Nothing attracts them strongly to each other; they are pushed together because water molecules, which hydrogen-bond to one another, exclude the non-polar tails.
items.misconception: The hydrophobic tails are held together by strong bonds that attract one hydrocarbon chain to another.
items.why: The phrase 'hydrophobic interactions' suggests an attraction between the tails, and students expect any stable structure to be held together by bonds between its parts. The forces between hydrocarbon tails are weak. The bilayer forms because water molecules hydrogen-bond to each other and to the hydrophilic heads, so the non-polar tails are excluded from the water and end up together. This exclusion is what drives the spontaneous self-assembly of vesicles.
items.specStatementText: Fatty acids self-assemble into vesicles
